results.summary: This design stores four characters in internal memory and displays them on a 16x4 LED matrix. It accepts four data bits and two position bits to load a hexadecimal character when the load signal is high, and otherwise cycles through the display columns using an internal character map. The design requires an external 16x4 LED matrix connected to the column and line outputs, and it must be reset before use. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation and interface.

This is a loopback test module that mirrors input 0 to outputs 0 through 6, and computes the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7 on output 7. It is intended for testing signal integrity and timing by toggling input 0 and measuring the delay until output 0 changes. The design has no external hardware requirements beyond the chip's pins. The documentation is minimal but clearly describes the function and test procedure.

This design implements an arithmetic logic unit that performs addition, multiplication, XOR, or shift-left on two 8-bit operands. Operands are entered via a 4x4 matrix keyboard, decoded and stored in a register bank, and the operation is selected by two input pins. The result is output on an 8-bit port, and the design includes a two-bit counter for keyboard scanning. The documentation describes the data flow and test procedure, but the pin names are somewhat cryptic and the design requires an external keyboard.

This design is a 2x2 systolic array tile for matrix multiplication, capable of streaming accumulation of a 2xN by Nx2 matrix product. It supports FP8 input formats and FP16 accumulators, with a pipelined multiply-accumulate operation and modes for passthrough, multiply-accumulate, and read-write of accumulators. The design is intended to be tiled in a grid, with data moving along rows and columns via 4-bit data and 1-bit control wires per direction. The documentation is extensive, including timing diagrams and example usage, but the design has not been tested in a full systolic array and safe clock speeds are unknown.

This design takes an 8-bit input and computes its factors, displaying them one by one on a seven-segment display with a one-second interval. It also indicates prime factors up to 19 on the bidirectional pins and uses the dot on the display to indicate primality. The design uses a modulo computation trick with hardcoded values and includes a clock divider to generate the one-second delay. Silicon testing confirmed it works, and the author notes it was a learning experience in hardware design.

This design is a hardware CPU for the brainfuck esolang with extensions for compressing consecutive operations. It uses an external asynchronous bus to access program and data memory, as well as I/O, since the memory does not fit on the chip. The bus protocol multiplexes address and data, and the CPU requires an external bus device, such as an RP2040, to operate. The documentation is detailed but the design is complex and requires careful integration with external hardware.

This design is an LED matrix driver that uses a counter and combinational logic to drive an 8x8 common anode LED matrix. It also outputs the lower 8 bits of the counter on bidirectional pins and drives a seven-segment display with the counter value. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the input pins to program a 24-bit compare value, with a default of one second per increment at 10 MHz. The documentation is brief but describes the operation and test procedure.

This design is an up-down counter that counts from 0 to 15 with options for enable, synchronous clear, and parallel load. It uses a clock divider to generate a 1 Hz counting rate from a 10 MHz input and decodes the count to BCD for display on a seven-segment display. The counter direction is controlled by an up input, and the load value is taken from four input pins. The documentation clearly explains the operation and test procedure.

ChipTune is an 8-bit programmable sound generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It features two rectangular pulse generators, a triangle wave generator, and a noise generator, each controlled by four 8-bit registers. Configuration data is received via a UART interface at 9600 baud, and the audio output is pulse-width modulated. The design requires an external analog PWM filter and audio driver for testing, and it can be interfaced with a computer COM port.

This is a simple 8-bit counter that was generated automatically by an Edge AI environment. It has no inputs and outputs the counter value on 8 pins. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it was generated by LLaMa2 and providing a link to the Edge Circuit Designer project. The design serves as a demonstration of AI-generated hardware.
